copy.subject: Their spot for season one is saved. Here's what's next.
copy.preview: Structure beats screen time limits. A note from our founder on what that looks like.
copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, I'm Karlin.

blocks.text: Thanks for joining the Season 01 waitlist. If our ad about screen time hit a little close to home, you're not alone. It's the reason I started EKUZO.
Like most kids, I cared most about video games and screens. And like most parents, mine thought they were the root of all my problems.
For the most part, they were right. Right up until I got a video game scholarship that paid for college.
Most families are constantly at war with screen time, stuck between taking it away and limiting it. I think there's a third option: give them a team and the tools to get better.
That's the structure of what we're building. A league where kids practice with legit coaches, rep a jersey with their gamer tag, and get better with their team every week.
This is less about screen time and more about your kid doing something they love, in a way that makes you proud.
Over the next few weeks, I'll show you exactly how it works: what practice looks like, what they learn, and what you'll see at home.
Glad you're here.

copy.ps: If you made it this far, you're the kind of parent we're building this for. Hit reply and tell me about your kid. I read every one.

copy.subject: Here's how it actually works
copy.preview: A team, a coach, and a night on the calendar. The short version.
copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, here's the short version.

blocks.text: A couple of days ago I told you why I started EKUZO. Today I want to show you what it actually is. It comes down to three things.

blocks.head: Build the team
blocks.text: Your kid joins a small team of kids around their age and level. Same teammates every week, a jersey with their gamer tag on it, and a team that has their back.

blocks.head: Meet the coach
blocks.text: Every practice is run by a coach who has played at a high level and chose to coach kids. They know the game. They also know the game is the easy part.

blocks.head: Practice
blocks.text: One night a week, on the calendar. It starts on time, it has a plan, and the coach ends it. Not you.
If your kid loves gaming, they're ready. Most kids start with a game they've never played, so everyone learns it together, with a coach, a team and a plan.
Over the next few emails I'll take these one at a time, starting with the team: who's on it, how it comes together, and why it matters more than the game.

copy.ps: What made you sign up? Something your kid said, or something you've been thinking about for a while? Hit reply. I read every one.

copy.subject: Here's what a practice night looks like
copy.preview: It starts on time, it has a plan, and the coach ends it. Not you.
copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, here's a practice night.

blocks.text: Last time I said I'd show you how this works. Here's one practice night, start to finish.

blocks.head: 6:55 · Logging in
blocks.text: Headset on. Their coach is already there, and so are the other kids on their team. Same kids every week, around the same age.

blocks.head: 7:00 · The plan
blocks.text: The coach opens with one thing the team is working on tonight. Not "get better." Something specific, like calling out what they see before it's too late.

blocks.head: 7:10 · Play
blocks.text: They play together while the coach listens to every call. This is the part you'll hear through the door.

blocks.head: 8:00 · The review
blocks.text: They watch back a moment from tonight, a fight they lost or a call that worked, and talk through why. Nobody gets blamed. Everyone leaves with one thing to try next week.

blocks.head: 8:30 · Done
blocks.text: The coach ends it. Not you.
That last part is the one parents tell us they didn't know they needed. The night has a start, a plan and an end, and someone other than you is holding the line.

copy.ps: Which night is the hardest one in your house when it comes to gaming? Hit reply and tell me. It'll help us pick Season 01 practice nights.
